mainEntity.name: Can people who grind their teeth still get porcelain veneers?

acceptedAnswer.text: Porcelain veneers may still be a suitable option for some patients who grind their teeth, but clinical assessment is essential before a decision is made. A dentist will evaluate the nature and severity of the bruxism, the condition of the underlying teeth, and the overall bite before advising on treatment suitability. In many cases, managing bruxism — for example with a custom nightguard — prior to or alongside veneer placement forms part of a responsible treatment approach. Individual circumstances vary significantly.

mainEntity.name: How long do porcelain veneers typically last?

acceptedAnswer.text: With good oral hygiene, regular dental care, and no significant parafunction (such as severe bruxism), porcelain veneers may last anywhere from 10 to 15 years or more. However, this is a general guide and not a guaranteed outcome for any individual patient. For those who grind their teeth, the lifespan may be shorter without appropriate protective measures. A dentist can provide a more personalised perspective based on a clinical assessment of your specific situation.

mainEntity.name: Will a nightguard completely protect my veneers from grinding damage?

acceptedAnswer.text: A well-fitted, custom occlusal nightguard is widely regarded as an effective way to reduce the mechanical forces imposed on veneers during grinding and clenching. However, it is important to understand that no single measure can guarantee complete protection. A nightguard reduces the risk of damage significantly and is a strongly recommended protective strategy, but it works best as part of a broader management plan that includes regular dental monitoring and good oral hygiene habits.

mainEntity.name: What happens if a porcelain veneer chips or breaks in a teeth grinder?

acceptedAnswer.text: If a veneer chips or breaks, it is advisable to contact your dental practice to arrange an assessment. Depending on the nature and extent of the damage, the veneer may be repaired, polished, or replaced. In some cases, the incident may prompt a review of occlusal management strategies — for example, ensuring a nightguard is being worn and that it fits correctly. Avoiding hard or crunchy foods in the interim and attending promptly for review is generally sensible.

mainEntity.name: Is bruxism a reason to avoid cosmetic dental treatment altogether?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not necessarily. Bruxism is a factor that requires careful consideration in treatment planning, but it does not automatically disqualify a patient from cosmetic dental treatment. The key is thorough clinical assessment, honest discussion between patient and clinician, and — where appropriate — putting protective measures in place before or alongside treatment. Patients with well-managed bruxism and realistic expectations may still achieve excellent long-term outcomes. Speaking openly with your dentist about your grinding habits is always the most constructive starting point.

mainEntity.name: Are there any alternative restorations better suited to teeth grinders?

acceptedAnswer.text: For some patients with significant bruxism, a dentist may discuss alternative restorations — such as composite bonding or dental crowns — which have different material properties and may suit certain clinical situations more appropriately. Composite restorations, for example, are generally easier to repair if damaged. Dental crowns offer greater coverage and may be recommended where a tooth has more substantial structural needs. The most suitable option will depend entirely on an individual's clinical assessment, and a detailed conversation with your dentist is the best way to explore all available choices.
